source: Heating can melt a solid into a liquid and turn a liquid into a gas. Cooling does the reverse. Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F) and boils at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level.
Thinking the steam you see over a pot is the gas. Water vapor is invisible; the white cloud is tiny drops of liquid water that formed as the vapor cooled.
Put an ice cube in a warm hand and it melts. Leave water in the freezer and it freezes. Heat a pot of water and it boils away. Matter can change state when it is heated or cooled.
Heating: solid → liquid is melting; liquid → gas is evaporating (or boiling, when it bubbles). Cooling: gas → liquid is condensing; liquid → solid is freezing.
Water freezes and ice melts at 0 °C (32 °F).

Heat makes particles move faster. When they move fast enough, they break out of their tight solid pattern (melting) or escape into the air (evaporating). Cooling slows them down so they stick together again.
A puddle is at −5 °C on a winter morning. Is it ice or water?
Thinking the white "steam" over a kettle is the gas. Water vapor is invisible. The white mist is tiny drops of liquid water made when the vapor cools in the air.
Melting does not change the mass. If 100 grams of ice melt, you have 100 grams of water.
